title: Thomas Beverage’s Tea Party connection is family tradition, not documented shipboard participation
summary: American Ancestors’ 2025 Boston Tea Party biographies list Thomas Beverage as an “Eyewitness.” The partner museum’s framework distinguishes eyewitnesses—people likely not aboard the ships but associated through family lore—from documented participants.
why_it_matters: This replaces a confident participation claim with the narrower conclusion the current evidence supports.

title: Published genealogy places the Thomas–Mercy marriage at Trinity Church
summary: An 1898 Kent family genealogy reports that Thomas Beverage and Mercy Kent married at Trinity Church in Boston on 13 April 1774.
why_it_matters: It supplies a traceable published source while clearly flagging that the original parish register still needs inspection.

title: Thomas Beverage appears in the earliest preserved plantation meeting record
summary: The 1889 Vinalhaven history says the earliest preserved plantation meeting was held at Benjamin Kent’s house on 11 March 1785 and that Thomas Beverage was chosen clerk.
why_it_matters: This supplies a dated civic role and corrects the site’s earlier, unsupported description of a land-petition meeting.

title: The 1790 census names Thomas but not the other ten household members
summary: The Vinalhaven transcription records “Thomas Beverege” with category counts of 2, 4, 5, 0, 0: two free white males 16 or older, four under 16, five free white females, no other free persons, and no enslaved people.
why_it_matters: The counts are evidence; assigning the unnamed entries to particular relatives is only a hypothesis and is now labeled that way.

title: The Mill Stream linked Thomas’s grist mill with James’s tannery
summary: North Haven Historical Society research says that by 1824 the Mill Stream site included a grist mill operated by Thomas Beverage, a tannery run by James Beverage, and a bark-grinding mill.
why_it_matters: It gives concrete occupational and place context for two generations of the family.

title: Harrison Beverage represented North Haven in 1859
summary: The 1889 Vinalhaven history records Harrison Beverage as North Haven’s chosen representative in 1859 and notes that he resigned before a December replacement election.
why_it_matters: It adds a documented public-service role to Harrison’s profile.

title: A compiled profile connects radio pioneer Harold Beverage to the North Haven branch
summary: A FamilySearch compiled profile identifies Fremont Beverage, son of Albert Glover Beverage and Olive Leadbetter Carver, as the husband of Lottie Henrietta Smith and father of Harold and three siblings.
why_it_matters: It closes a missing branch in the website’s data, but the relationship is deliberately marked provisional until original record images are reviewed.

sources.title: Find A Grave memorial: Harold Henry Beverage

title: Harold Beverage’s 1921 patent documents the directional receiving system
summary: U.S. Patent 1,381,089 names Harold H. Beverage as inventor of a radio receiving system filed in 1920 and issued on 7 June 1921. The long-wire arrangement was designed for strong directional selectivity in reception.
why_it_matters: It anchors the family story in an original invention record and explains why the Beverage name is familiar to radio operators.

sources.title: IEEE Engineering and Technology History Wiki: Harold H. Beverage

title: IEEE’s oral history preserves Harold Beverage’s North Haven recollections
summary: In an IEEE oral history, Harold described growing up on a North Haven farm, repairing island telephones at about age fourteen, studying electrical engineering at the University of Maine, and entering the emerging field of long-distance radio.
why_it_matters: The interview adds first-person context that cannot be recovered from vital records alone, while memories are still treated as testimony rather than independent proof.
